prompt: What does a card's column on the board say?
hint: Each column has a rule for entering it.

choices.why: Importance is the order within to do, not the column.

choices.text: What state the work is in now
choices.why: Right. Anybody can read the board without asking.
The initials on a card are who is doing it.

choices.text: How long the work will take
choices.why: That is an estimate, lesson 16.

prompt: Who should move Ana's card from in progress to in review?
hint: A board updated weekly shows last week.

choices.text: The product owner, at the review
choices.why: By then the board has been wrong for days.
A weekly update makes the board a picture of the past.

choices.text: Ana, when it changes, or the tool
choices.why: Right. Many tools move it when the pull request opens.
The reviewer may not know it is ready yet.

prompt: Bruno's card #36 is marked blocked. What is that for?
hint: It is information, not a confession.

choices.text: To record that Bruno is behind
choices.why: It records the card's state, not a judgement.

choices.text: To take the card off the board
choices.why: It stays where it is, marked.

choices.text: To reassign the ticket to somebody else
choices.why: Nobody else can continue either; it waits for the host.

choices.text: So the team sees it and helps out
choices.why: Right. A stuck card nobody knows about stays stuck.

prompt: Ana finishes #34. In progress and in review are both at their limit of 2. What should she do next?
hint: Move cards to the right before adding any on the left.

choices.text: Start #35, the top of to do
choices.why: In progress is full; starting adds to the pile.
Right. That moves cards to done and frees a slot.
Raising it whenever it bites removes its point.
There is useful work right now: reviewing.

prompt: Why does a WIP limit make a team deliver sooner?
hint: What is five half-done things worth to a customer?

choices.text: It makes everybody work longer hours
choices.why: It changes what people work on, not how long.
The unfinished work is exactly what it exposes.
Right. Half-done work is worth nothing, and switching costs time.
Tickets can still be written; they wait in to do.

prompt: Match each Scrum term to what it is.

pairs.right: Everything wanted, in order of importance
What the team agreed to do this sprint
One sentence saying what the sprint is for
A fixed stretch of time, often two weeks

right_distractors: The time from starting a card to finishing it

prompt: Halfway through a sprint it is clear not every ticket will fit. What helps the team decide which to drop?

choices.why: Right. Keep what serves it; drop what does not.
Age says nothing about what matters.
The goal already answers it.
Length is not importance.

prompt: Put a sprint's events in the order they happen.
hint: The retro looks back at a finished sprint.
trap: A retro before the review changes the process before the team has seen what the sprint produced.

prompt: Match each Scrum role to what it decides or does.
hint: One description is nobody's job in Scrum.

pairs.right: What is most important, and why
How to build it, and how much fits

right_distractors: Assigning tickets to people each morning

prompt: A week into a sprint, a manager asks for a new page by Friday. It is not urgent. What usually happens?
hint: What does the sprint's boundary protect?

choices.text: The team drops everything for it
choices.why: Then the sprint goal was never protected.
It is not refused; it waits for the next planning.

choices.text: It goes to the backlog for next planning
choices.why: Right. At most two weeks away.
Hidden work is the thing a board exists to prevent.

prompt: In kanban nobody pushes work at a developer. When they finish a card, they ___ the next one from the top of to do.
Match each measure to what it spans.

pairs.right: From the ticket being written to done
From somebody starting it to done

prompt: Cycle time is long, and most cards spend days in review. What is often the answer?

choices.why: The wait is inside the board, not at its edges.
That lengthens lead time and fixes nothing.
That removes the queue by removing the safety net.
Right. People then review before starting more.

prompt: A support team's work is decided each day by what breaks. Which fits better?
hint: Can this work be planned two weeks ahead?

choices.why: A one-day sprint is planning overhead with no horizon.
Right. Work is pulled as it arrives.
The board is where the work would be seen.
Unpredictable work needs a limit more, not less.

prompt: Which questions does the lesson suggest asking in your first week? Choose all that apply.
hint: They find out which parts the team kept.

choices.why: Yes. And whether any has a limit.
Yes. Lesson 17.

choices.text: Which method is the correct one?
choices.why: Neither is correct in general; ask what they do.

choices.text: How long is a sprint, if there is one?
choices.why: Yes. And what happens at its start and end.

choices.text: Why do you not use Scrum by the book?
choices.why: Almost nobody does; it is not a question to open with.

prompt: We are halfway through the sprint, the board is full, and your ticket is blocked. What is the most useful reply?
hint: A full board means finish, not start.

choices.text: I'll start the next ticket in to do
choices.why: The board is full; starting adds to it.

choices.text: I'll wait until it is unblocked
choices.why: Waiting idle helps nobody while reviews queue.

choices.text: Can I help finish something in review?
choices.why: Right. That moves the board and uses the time.

choices.text: Can we move my ticket back to to do?
choices.why: Its state is blocked; hiding that loses the information.

prompt: Which of these are true? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: In kanban, the WIP limit is the mechanism
choices.why: Yes. Without it the board is a growing list.

choices.text: A sprint's scope can grow freely once it starts
choices.why: The goal is protected; requests wait.

choices.text: The product owner decides how to build it
choices.why: They decide what and why; developers decide how.

choices.text: Many teams mix Scrum's rhythm with kanban's limits
choices.why: Yes. Sometimes called scrumban.
